questions.stem: What compression rate and depth define high-quality CPR in an adult?
questions.why: 100 to 120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, full recoil between compressions, minimal interruptions, and no over-ventilation. Nothing else in an arrest matters as much as getting these right.

options.t: 100 to 120 per minute, at least 2 inches deep
60 to 80 per minute, as deep as the chest allows
options.why: That rate is far too slow, and depth beyond 2.4 inches causes injury.

options.t: 80 to 100 per minute, at least 1 inch deep
options.why: Both figures fall short — that rate and depth do not generate adequate flow.

options.t: 120 to 140 per minute, about 1.5 inches deep
options.why: Faster than 120 shortens recoil time, and 1.5 inches is too shallow.

questions.stem: Why does full chest recoil between compressions matter?
questions.why: Compression pushes blood out; recoil is what draws it back in. Leaning on the chest keeps intrathoracic pressure up, blocks venous return, and quietly halves the effectiveness of every compression that follows.

options.t: It lets the defibrillator read the rhythm between beats
options.why: Rhythm analysis requires pausing compressions entirely.

options.t: It allows the rescuer to keep the rate up over time
options.why: Recoil is about the patient's physiology, not the rescuer's stamina.

options.t: It reduces the risk of fracturing ribs during compressions
options.why: Rib fracture relates to depth and hand position, not to recoil.

options.t: Recoil creates the negative pressure that refills

questions.stem: Once an advanced airway is in place during an arrest, how should ventilations be delivered?
questions.why: With an advanced airway, compressions run continuously and ventilations go in at about 10 per minute — one every 6 seconds. Over-ventilation is one of the most common and most damaging errors in an arrest.

options.t: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, with a pause for each pair
options.why: That ratio applies before an advanced airway is placed.

options.t: One breath every 6 seconds, without pausing compressions
Continuous ventilation matched to the compression rate
options.why: Ventilating with every compression would grossly over-ventilate the patient.

options.t: One breath every 3 seconds, to maximize oxygenation
options.why: Twenty breaths a minute raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return.

questions.stem: What is the physiologic harm of over-ventilating a patient in cardiac arrest?
questions.why: Each positive-pressure breath raises pressure inside the chest, which squeezes the great veins and reduces the blood available for the next compression to move. It directly lowers coronary perfusion pressure.

options.t: Blowing off CO2 alkalizes the blood and stops the heart
options.why: Alkalosis is undesirable but it is not the main mechanism of harm here.

options.t: Oxygen toxicity develops in the alveoli within minutes
options.why: Oxygen toxicity is a long-exposure problem, not a resuscitation-timescale one.

options.t: Rising intrathoracic pressure cuts venous return
The stomach inflates and the patient vomits every time
options.why: Gastric insufflation is a real risk but secondary to the hemodynamic effect.

questions.stem: What does an EtCO2 that suddenly jumps from 12 to 40 during compressions suggest?
questions.why: EtCO2 tracks cardiac output during CPR. An abrupt rise means blood is circulating again — often the first sign of ROSC, and one you get without stopping compressions to check a pulse.

options.t: The endotracheal tube has become dislodged
options.why: A dislodged tube causes the waveform to disappear.

options.t: Return of spontaneous circulation
The patient is being over-ventilated
options.why: Over-ventilation drives EtCO2 down by washing out CO2.

options.t: The compressions have become too shallow to move blood
options.why: Poor compressions would lower EtCO2, not raise it.

questions.stem: What does a persistently low EtCO2 — under 10 — after 20 minutes of resuscitation indicate?
questions.why: Under 10 after 20 minutes of good CPR means very little blood is reaching the lungs. It is one of the few objective inputs into a decision about terminating resuscitation — never the only one.

options.t: Successful ventilation with adequate CO2 clearance
options.why: Adequate clearance requires circulation to deliver the CO2 in the first place.

options.t: Poor perfusion and a poor prognosis
An equipment fault requiring a new sensor
options.why: A fault produces no waveform at all rather than a low steady number.

options.t: Effective compressions producing adequate circulation
options.why: Effective compressions typically produce values well above 10.

questions.stem: What does defibrillation actually accomplish?
questions.why: Defibrillation stops everything at once. The hope is that when the myocardium repolarizes, the fastest intrinsic pacemaker — normally the SA node — resumes control of an organized rhythm.

options.t: It depolarizes the whole myocardium at once
It stimulates the SA node directly to fire again
options.why: The current passes through the whole myocardium, not selectively to the node.

options.t: It improves coronary perfusion during the shock itself
options.why: Perfusion comes from compressions; the shock is momentary.

options.t: It restarts a heart that has stopped beating entirely
options.why: A shock stops chaotic activity; it does not start a heart that has none.

questions.stem: What should happen immediately after a shock is delivered?
questions.why: Even a successful shock leaves a stunned myocardium that takes time to generate a pulse. Compressions resume immediately and continue for a full two-minute cycle before the next rhythm check.

options.t: Resume compressions at once, no pulse check
Reanalyze the rhythm to confirm the shock worked
options.why: Reanalyzing straight away costs compression time and usually shows nothing useful yet.

options.t: Check for a pulse for up to ten seconds
options.why: A pulse check right after a shock wastes perfusion time; the heart rarely produces one immediately.

options.t: Give epinephrine before restarting compressions
options.why: Drugs go in during compressions, not in place of them.

questions.stem: Per the program's VF/pulseless VT algorithm, what energy is delivered on the first shock?
questions.why: The algorithm escalates: 150 biphasic / 200 monophasic, then 200 / 300, then 200 / 360 and every shock after. The Field Code lecture gives the general AED default as 200 joules with an acceptable range of 120 to 200 — know the algorithm numbers for the exam.

options.t: 150 joules biphasic, 200 joules monophasic
Whatever the manufacturer lists, with no fixed first energy
options.why: The program's algorithm fixes the first energy rather than deferring to the device.

options.t: 200 joules biphasic, 300 joules monophasic
options.why: Those are the second-shock energies in the algorithm, not the first.

options.t: 360 joules monophasic on the first attempt
options.why: 360 monophasic is reached on the third shock, after two lower attempts.

questions.stem: What does the sync function do in synchronized cardioversion?
questions.why: The shock has to miss the T wave. Landing on it during the relative refractory period can drive the patient into ventricular fibrillation — which is the whole reason synchronization exists.

options.t: It lowers the delivered energy automatically
options.why: Energy is set by the operator; sync governs timing only.

options.t: It times the shock to the R wave
It analyzes the rhythm and decides whether to shock
options.why: That is an AED's advisory function, not synchronization.

options.t: It delivers a series of small shocks instead of one
options.why: Synchronized cardioversion delivers a single timed shock.

questions.stem: You press shock in sync mode and nothing is delivered. What is the most likely reason?
questions.why: Sync mode will not fire without a clear R wave. Increase the gain, change leads, or check pad contact — and if the patient is pulseless, turn sync off and defibrillate.

options.t: The patient's rhythm has already converted
options.why: A converted rhythm still has R waves for the device to track.

options.t: The pads have been placed in the wrong position
options.why: Bad placement gives a poor shock, not an absent one.

options.t: The device cannot find R waves to synchronize to
The energy setting is below the device's minimum
options.why: The device would deliver its minimum rather than nothing at all.

questions.stem: In the program's VF/pulseless VT algorithm, at what point in the sequence is the first epinephrine given?
questions.why: The order is: shock, CPR + IV/IO, shock, CPR + 1 mg epi 1:10,000 and consider an advanced airway, shock, CPR + 300 mg amiodarone and treat the Hs and Ts. Epinephrine then repeats every three to five minutes.

options.t: Only after amiodarone has failed to convert the rhythm
options.why: Epinephrine comes before the antidysrhythmic, not after it.

options.t: During the CPR cycle after the first shock
options.why: The cycle after the first shock is CPR plus IV/IO access — no drug yet.

options.t: Before the first shock, as soon as the rhythm is identified
options.why: Defibrillation is the treatment for a shockable rhythm; the first two shocks come before any drug.

options.t: During the CPR cycle after the second shock

questions.stem: An unstable patient needs cardioversion but is awake and frightened. What should you do?
questions.why: Sedate when you can — cardioversion is painful and the patient is awake. But sedation must not delay the shock in a patient who is deteriorating; the clinical picture sets that balance.

options.t: Cardiovert immediately without sedation in every unstable case
options.why: Where there is time, sedation is both humane and standard.

options.t: Attempt vagal maneuvers instead, to avoid the shock
options.why: Vagal maneuvers are for the stable patient with a narrow-complex tachycardia.

options.t: Sedate if time and their condition allow, then cardiovert
Delay cardioversion until full sedation has been achieved
options.why: A crashing patient cannot wait for ideal sedation.

questions.stem: How do you confirm that transcutaneous pacing is capturing?
questions.why: Electrical capture is a wide QRS following each spike. Mechanical capture is a pulse that matches the paced rate. Both are required — a twitching patient with no pulse is not being paced effectively.

options.t: The set rate appearing on the monitor display
options.why: The display shows what was programmed, not what the patient's heart did.

options.t: A pacer spike appearing before every complex
options.why: Spikes only show the device is firing, not that the heart answered.

options.t: The patient's muscles twitching with each impulse
options.why: Muscle twitch means current is passing through tissue, not that the myocardium captured.

options.t: A wide QRS after each spike, with a pulse

questions.stem: How should the milliamp setting be established when starting transcutaneous pacing?
questions.why: Bring the current up from low until you see electrical and mechanical capture, then set it slightly above that threshold. Higher than necessary is needlessly painful; lower loses capture the moment anything shifts.

options.t: Start at maximum output and reduce until capture is lost
options.why: Starting at maximum is unnecessarily painful and offers no advantage.

options.t: Match the milliamps to the patient's weight in kilograms
options.why: There is no weight-based formula for pacing output.

options.t: Use a fixed 80 mA for every adult patient
options.why: Capture thresholds vary widely between patients.

options.t: Increase until capture, then add a small margin above it

questions.stem: Per the program's drug sheet, what is the atropine dose for unstable bradycardia?
questions.why: The drug sheet gives 1 mg IV/IO every three to five minutes to a 3 mg maximum for unstable bradycardia. Atropine is an anticholinergic — it blocks vagal tone at the AV node rather than stimulating the heart directly.

options.t: 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes, to a total of 3 mg
1 mg IV/IO once only, with no repeat dose
options.why: The sheet allows repeat dosing up to a 3 mg total.

options.t: 0.5 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes, to a total of 3 mg
options.why: 0.5 mg is a dose used in some protocols, but the program's sheet specifies 1 mg.

options.t: 2 to 4 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes
options.why: That range is the organophosphate poisoning dose, not the bradycardia dose.

questions.stem: Why is atropine unlikely to help in third-degree block with a wide escape rhythm?
questions.why: Atropine blocks vagal tone at the AV node. In a high-grade infranodal block the problem sits below that, so removing vagal influence changes nothing — pacing, or an epinephrine infusion, is the answer.

options.t: Atropine slows conduction rather than speeding it
options.why: Atropine speeds AV conduction — it is positive dromotropic.

options.t: The lesion is below the node where atropine acts
Complete block makes the myocardium unresponsive to any drug
options.why: The myocardium still responds to catecholamines and to pacing.

options.t: The dose required would exceed the safe maximum
options.why: Dose is not the limitation; the site of action is.

questions.stem: Per the drug sheet, what is push-dose epinephrine used for and at what dose?
questions.why: Push-dose epinephrine is a small, dilute, titratable dose for a patient who has a pulse but not enough pressure — symptomatic bradycardia, beta blocker or calcium channel overdose, and post-ROSC hypotension.

options.t: 1 mg of 1:10,000 every 3 to 5 minutes until pressure improves
options.why: That is the cardiac arrest dose, far too much for a patient with a pulse.

options.t: 5 to 20 mcg of 1:100,000 every 2 to 5 minutes
0.3 mg of 1:1,000 IM, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes
options.why: That is the anaphylaxis dose and route.

options.t: 40 units IV/IO as a single dose
options.why: That describes vasopressin, not epinephrine.

questions.stem: Per the drug sheet, what is the adult epinephrine dose in cardiac arrest?
questions.why: One milligram of 1:10,000 — 10 mL of the prefilled syringe — every three to five minutes. Its value in arrest comes from alpha-mediated vasoconstriction, which raises coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during compressions.

options.t: 1 mg of 1:10,000 IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes
1 mg of 1:1,000 IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes
options.why: 1:1,000 is the concentration used intramuscularly for anaphylaxis.

options.t: 0.5 mg of 1:10,000 IV/IO every 5 minutes
options.why: The arrest dose is a full milligram.

options.t: 1 mg of 1:10,000 IV/IO as a single dose only
options.why: It is repeated every three to five minutes for the duration of the arrest.

questions.stem: Per the drug sheet, how is amiodarone dosed in refractory VF or pulseless VT?
questions.why: In arrest: 300 mg push, then 150 mg. In a stable wide-complex tachycardia the same drug is given as 150 mg slowly over ten minutes — same drug, different urgency, different delivery.

options.t: 150 mg slow IV/IO over 10 minutes, repeated as needed
options.why: That is the stable wide-complex tachycardia dose, given to a patient with a pulse.

options.t: 150 mg IV/IO push, then 300 mg in 3 to 5 minutes
options.why: That reverses the two doses — the larger one comes first.

options.t: 300 mg IV/IO push, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes
options.why: The second dose is half the first, and it is given once.

options.t: 300 mg IV/IO push, then 150 mg in 3 to 5 minutes

questions.stem: Per the drug sheet, how may vasopressin be used in cardiac arrest?
questions.why: Vasopressin is given as a single 40-unit dose replacing the first or second epinephrine. It is a non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor, which is why it can substitute for epinephrine's alpha effect.

options.t: 40 units IV/IO repeated every 5 minutes as needed
options.why: The sheet describes it as a single one-time dose.

options.t: 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes alongside epinephrine
options.why: 1 mg every three to five minutes is the epinephrine regimen.

options.t: 40 units IV/IO in place of the first or second epi
40 units IV/IO in addition to every epinephrine dose
options.why: It substitutes for a dose rather than adding to the sequence.

questions.stem: Per the drug sheet, what is the adult lidocaine dose for VF or pulseless VT?
questions.why: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg initially, then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg every five minutes to a total of 3 mg/kg. Lidocaine is the alternative when amiodarone is unavailable or contraindicated.

options.t: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg, then half doses to 3 mg/kg
3 mg/kg IV/IO as the initial loading dose
options.why: 3 mg/kg is the cumulative maximum, not the first dose.

options.t: 0.5 mg/kg IV/IO, to a maximum of 40 mg
options.why: That is the dose used for IO insertion pain in a conscious patient.

options.t: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg IV/IO as a single dose with no repeat
options.why: Repeat half-doses are part of the regimen up to the 3 mg/kg ceiling.

questions.stem: Which reversible cause of arrest is most directly suggested by a widened QRS and peaked T waves before the arrest?
questions.why: Hyperkalemia peaks the T waves, flattens the P waves and widens the QRS toward a sine wave. It is one of the most treatable causes of arrest, especially in a dialysis patient or a crush injury.

options.t: Hypothermia
options.why: Hypothermia classically produces Osborn J waves and a slow rate.

options.t: Tension pneumothorax
options.why: That presents with absent breath sounds, distended neck veins and tracheal shift, not a specific ECG pattern.

options.t: Hyperkalemia
Hypovolemia
options.why: Hypovolemia narrows pulse pressure and raises the rate; it does not peak T waves.

questions.stem: A dialysis patient arrests in PEA. Which reversible causes should be at the top of your list?
questions.why: Missed dialysis means potassium climbs, and a session just finished means volume was pulled off. Both, plus the underlying acidosis, are correctable — which is exactly why the Hs and Ts get worked systematically.

options.t: Thrombosis of the coronary arteries alone
options.why: Coronary disease is common in these patients, but it does not lead the list in a PEA arrest.

options.t: Hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, and acidosis
Tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade
options.why: Those are trauma and pericardial problems rather than dialysis-specific ones.

options.t: Hypothermia and toxins from the dialysate
options.why: Both are possible but far less likely than the electrolyte and volume problems dialysis creates.

questions.stem: Per the program's post-resuscitation care, what blood pressure is targeted and how is it supported?
questions.why: After ROSC: stabilize the rhythm, support pressure with dopamine or norepinephrine to a systolic of at least 100, raise the head 30 degrees, obtain a 12-lead, check glucose, prevent seizures, and use targeted temperature management for the patient who stays comatose.

options.t: Systolic at least 100, using fluid boluses alone
options.why: Vasopressors are named in the post-resuscitation care, not fluid alone.

options.t: Systolic at least 100, using dopamine or norepinephrine
Mean arterial pressure at least 65, using dopamine
options.why: The program teaches a systolic target of 100 rather than a MAP number.

options.t: Whatever the pressure was before the arrest
options.why: Pre-arrest pressure is normally unknown and is not the target taught.

questions.stem: Why should oxygen be titrated rather than left at 100 percent after ROSC?
questions.why: Reperfused tissue generates free radicals, and excess oxygen feeds that injury. Titrate to a saturation in the mid-90s rather than leaving the patient on 100 percent.

options.t: High oxygen suppresses the respiratory drive in these patients
options.why: A post-arrest patient is usually being ventilated; their own drive is not the concern.

options.t: Pulse oximetry becomes unreliable at high concentrations
options.why: Oximetry works at high saturations; it simply cannot distinguish above 100 percent.

options.t: It preserves oxygen supply for a possible second arrest
options.why: Supply conservation is not a clinical reason to under-oxygenate.

options.t: Hyperoxia after reperfusion worsens oxidative injury

questions.stem: Which patient after ROSC is the candidate for targeted temperature management?
questions.why: TTM targets the comatose ROSC patient, where the goal is limiting the brain injury caused by the arrest. Prehospital, the practical point is not to actively rewarm these patients.

options.t: Only the patient whose arrest was witnessed
options.why: Whether the arrest was witnessed does not decide temperature management.

options.t: The patient who remains comatose
Any ROSC patient, whatever their mental status
options.why: A patient who wakes up and follows commands is not a candidate.

options.t: Only the patient who arrested from a shockable rhythm
options.why: The initial rhythm does not exclude a comatose patient from temperature management.

questions.stem: What does closed-loop communication mean during a resuscitation?
questions.why: Name the person, state the order, hear it repeated back, and hear that it was done. It is how a team catches the drug that was never given and the shock that was never delivered.

options.t: Orders are given to the room rather than to an individual
options.why: Unassigned orders are exactly what closed-loop communication prevents.

options.t: Every order is written down before it is carried out
options.why: Documentation matters, but it is not what closes the loop in real time.

options.t: The receiver repeats the order back and reports it done
Only the team leader speaks during the resuscitation
options.why: Silencing the team removes the input the leader depends on.

questions.stem: Why should the compressor be rotated every two minutes?
questions.why: Depth and recoil degrade within a couple of minutes, and the person compressing is usually the last to know. The switch happens during the rhythm check so it costs no extra pause.

options.t: It reduces the risk of injury to the rescuer's back
options.why: Rescuer strain is real but is not the reason for the interval.

options.t: Two minutes is the maximum a defibrillator will analyze for
options.why: Two-minute cycles align with rhythm checks, but the reason for switching is fatigue.

options.t: Compression quality falls off before the rescuer notices
It gives each team member a chance to assess the patient
options.why: Assessment happens continuously; rotation is not the mechanism for it.

questions.stem: Per the program's criteria, which combination supports terminating resuscitation in the field?
questions.why: All four must be true: the arrest was unwitnessed, no bystander CPR was given, the AED never advised a shock, and there is no ROSC after three rounds of ALS medications. The PEA/asystole algorithm frames the same idea as three rounds of ALS medications or 20 minutes of CPR.

options.t: Unwitnessed arrest in a patient over 70
options.why: Age is not one of the criteria taught.

options.t: Unwitnessed, no bystander CPR, no shocks, no ROSC after three rounds
No ROSC after two rounds of ALS medications
options.why: The criterion is three rounds of ALS medications, not two.

options.t: A rhythm of asystole at any point during the arrest
options.why: Asystole appearing at some point is not by itself a reason to stop.

questions.stem: Match each reversible cause of arrest to its most suggestive clue.
questions.why: PEA and asystole are not treated by treating the rhythm — they are treated by finding the cause. The Hs and Ts are a checklist so nothing correctable gets skipped.
pairs: Trauma, GI bleed, or a narrow pulse pressure beforehand
Respiratory arrest that preceded the cardiac arrest
Dialysis patient, or peaked T waves before the arrest
Absent breath sounds with distended neck veins
Muffled tones, distended neck veins, narrow pulse pressure
Sudden collapse with recent immobility or surgery

questions.stem: Match each electrical therapy to the situation it belongs in.
questions.why: Two questions sort almost all of it: does the patient have a pulse, and is the rate too fast or too slow? The answers pick the therapy.
pairs: Symptomatic bradycardia not responding to atropine

questions.stem: After how many shocks does the program's algorithm call for the first antidysrhythmic?
questions.why: Shock one, then CPR and access. Shock two, then epinephrine. Shock three, then 300 mg amiodarone and the Hs and Ts. The second amiodarone dose of 150 mg follows two shocks later, and after that the algorithm says no more amiodarone.

options.t: After the third shock
After the fifth shock
options.why: By the fifth shock the second, smaller amiodarone dose is already due.

options.t: After the first shock
options.why: The cycle after the first shock is CPR and IV/IO access only.

options.t: After the second shock
options.why: The cycle after the second shock is where epinephrine goes in.

questions.stem: A patient in arrest is wearing a transdermal medication patch on the chest where a pad belongs. What should you do?
questions.why: A patch under a pad can arc, burn the skin and block current. Peel it off, wipe the residue away, and place the pad properly — it takes a couple of seconds.

options.t: Remove the patch, wipe the skin, and place the pad
Place the pad directly over the patch to save time
options.why: Current can arc across the patch's backing and burn the skin.

options.t: Leave the patch and reduce the delivered energy
options.why: Reducing energy risks a failed shock and does nothing about the arcing.

options.t: Move the pad to the abdomen instead
options.why: Moving off the correct position degrades the shock vector through the heart.

questions.stem: What is the target for chest compression fraction during a resuscitation?
questions.why: Compression fraction is the share of the arrest spent actually compressing. Every pause — for intubation, for a pulse check, for moving the patient — drops coronary perfusion pressure that takes several compressions to rebuild.

options.t: Fraction is not tracked during prehospital resuscitation
options.why: Many monitors record it, and it is one of the strongest quality measures there is.

options.t: At least 60 percent of the time, ideally above 80
At least 30 percent, allowing time for interventions
options.why: Thirty percent means the chest is idle most of the arrest.

options.t: Exactly 50 percent, split evenly with ventilation
options.why: Compressions do not pause for ventilation once an advanced airway is in.

questions.stem: How many total doses of amiodarone does the program's VF/VT algorithm allow?
questions.why: 300 mg after the third shock, 150 mg two shocks later, then the algorithm explicitly says no more amiodarone — epinephrine continues every three to five minutes but the antidysrhythmic does not.

options.t: One — a single 300 mg dose only
options.why: A second, smaller dose follows if the arrest continues.

options.t: Three — 300 mg, then 150 mg, then 150 mg
options.why: The algorithm stops after the second dose and states no more amiodarone.

options.t: Two — 300 mg, then 150 mg
As many 150 mg doses as the arrest lasts
options.why: There is a hard ceiling of two doses in this algorithm.

questions.stem: Amiodarone is unavailable and you reach for lidocaine. What must you not do?
questions.why: Lidocaine is 1 to 1.5 mg/kg, then 0.5 to 0.75 mg/kg, to a maximum of three doses or 3 mg/kg. It is an alternative to amiodarone, never an addition — the two are not combined.

options.t: Give it through an intraosseous line
options.why: IO is an accepted route for it in arrest.

options.t: Give it before epinephrine has been started
options.why: The antidysrhythmic follows epinephrine in the sequence either way.

options.t: Give a repeat dose after the first
options.why: Repeat half-doses are part of the regimen, up to three doses or 3 mg/kg.

options.t: Combine it with amiodarone

questions.stem: A patient in arrest shows polymorphic VT with a twisting axis. Which drug replaces amiodarone?
questions.why: Torsades de pointes gets magnesium 1 to 2 grams IV/IO in place of amiodarone. Defibrillation and CPR continue unchanged — the drug substitution is the only difference.

options.t: Calcium chloride 1 g IV/IO
options.why: Calcium is for hyperkalemia and calcium-channel-blocker overdose, not torsades.

options.t: A second dose of epinephrine given early
options.why: Epinephrine continues on its own schedule and does not treat the twisting itself.

options.t: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV/IO
options.why: Bicarbonate addresses acidosis and tricyclic overdose, not torsades.

options.t: Magnesium sulfate 1 to 2 g IV/IO

questions.stem: You arrive at an unwitnessed arrest with an AED. What does the program teach you to do first?
questions.why: An unwitnessed arrest gets five cycles of CPR first, to perfuse a heart that has been down long enough to have exhausted its energy stores. A witnessed arrest is analyzed and shocked as soon as the AED is on.

options.t: Five cycles of CPR before applying the AED
Two minutes of ventilation, then analyze
options.why: Compressions, not ventilation alone, are what precede the analysis.

options.t: Establish an advanced airway before any analysis
options.why: The airway is not what delays the first analysis in an unwitnessed arrest.

options.t: Apply the AED and analyze immediately
options.why: Immediate analysis is for the witnessed arrest, where the heart still has substrate to shock.

questions.stem: Why must the ventilation device be removed from the patient before a shock is delivered?
questions.why: Oxygen flowing across the chest during an arc is a fire risk. Take the device off the patient, then clear and shock.

options.t: It prevents the chest from recoiling between compressions
options.why: Recoil is a compression concern and unrelated to the shock itself.

options.t: It interferes with the monitor's rhythm analysis
options.why: The device does not corrupt the analysis; the hazard is physical.

options.t: Flowing oxygen at the airway is a fire hazard
It transmits current back to the rescuer holding it
options.why: The bag is not a conductive path back to the rescuer.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old in VF is being defibrillated. What are the first and second energies?
questions.why: Pediatric defibrillation is weight-based: 2 J/kg first, 4 J/kg after. Pediatric epinephrine in this algorithm goes in only after two shocks, with the dose doubled.

options.t: 2 J/kg, then 2 J/kg repeated
options.why: The second attempt doubles rather than repeating the first energy.

options.t: 4 J/kg, then 8 J/kg
options.why: 4 J/kg is the second dose, not the first.

options.t: 1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg
options.why: Both figures are half the pediatric energies taught.

options.t: 2 J/kg, then 4 J/kg

questions.stem: When are anterior-posterior pad placement and a pediatric attenuator indicated?
questions.why: Under one year or under 22 pounds: anterior-posterior placement with an attenuator. Other special circumstances on the same list — shave a hairy chest, dry a wet patient, stay a few inches off an AICD, and remove a medication patch.

options.t: Only when an adult AED is the sole device available
options.why: The attenuator is what adapts an adult AED; the criterion is still the child's size.

options.t: Under eight years of age or under 55 pounds
options.why: Eight years is the older cutoff for pediatric pads generally, not for AP placement here.

options.t: Under one year of age or under 22 pounds
Any time the chest is too small for two pads to sit flat
options.why: The teaching point is a stated age and weight, not a judgment call.

questions.stem: What EtCO2 range does the program expect during effective CPR?
questions.why: 10 to 20 during compressions is the working target. A sustained rise above 40 is the capnography signature of ROSC — check a pulse rather than stopping to look at the monitor.

options.t: 20 to 40 mmHg
options.why: That range is closer to a perfusing patient than to one receiving compressions.

options.t: Under 10 mmHg
options.why: Under 10 signals compressions that are not moving enough blood.

options.t: 35 to 45 mmHg
options.why: That is the normal range for a patient with a pulse and normal ventilation.

options.t: 10 to 20 mmHg

questions.stem: How much interruption in compressions is acceptable while placing an advanced airway?
questions.why: Under ten seconds. The same ceiling governs pulse checks and rhythm analysis — compression fraction is the number that predicts survival.

options.t: As long as the attempt takes, since the airway is definitive
options.why: No airway attempt outranks perfusion during an arrest.

options.t: Less than 10 seconds
Less than 30 seconds
options.why: Thirty seconds is far longer than the interruption this program allows.

options.t: No interruption is acceptable under any circumstance
options.why: A brief pause under ten seconds is permitted.

questions.stem: Which task belongs to the code team leader rather than to a team member?
questions.why: The leader assigns roles, keeps the algorithm moving, watches the clock and the monitor, makes the medication and transport decisions, and speaks for the team — the hands-on tasks belong to the members.

options.t: Managing the airway and ventilations
options.why: Airway is a separately assigned role.

options.t: Assigning roles and directing the resuscitation
Delivering compressions during the first two-minute cycle
options.why: The leader stays free to direct rather than taking a hands-on role.

options.t: Establishing the IV or IO access
options.why: Access is a team member's assignment.

questions.stem: How many links does the chain of survival taught in this program have?
questions.why: Five links. The lecture puts the chance of ROSC at roughly 40 percent when the whole chain functions — the point being that no single link carries the outcome.

options.t: Four
options.why: Four is the older version of the chain.

options.t: Three
options.why: Three is fewer than any published version of the chain.

options.t: Five
Six
options.why: Six overshoots the version taught here.

questions.stem: Which finding permits withholding resuscitation as an obvious death?
questions.why: Rigor mortis, dependent lividity, putrefaction, and injuries incompatible with life. Everything short of that gets a resuscitation.

options.t: Dependent lividity
Fixed and dilated pupils
options.why: Pupils can be fixed and dilated in a patient who is still resuscitatable.

options.t: Asystole in three leads
options.why: Asystole is a rhythm to work, not a sign of irreversible death.

options.t: A core temperature well below normal
options.why: The cold patient is warmed and worked — nobody is dead until warm and dead.

questions.stem: What does the thoracic pump theory say produces blood flow during compressions?
questions.why: Two explanations are taught side by side: the heart pump theory has the heart squeezed directly between sternum and spine, the thoracic pump theory has the whole chest acting as a pressure chamber.

options.t: Recoil of the ribs drawing blood into the atria
options.why: Recoil matters for filling but is not what this theory names as the driver.

options.t: Ventilations raising pulmonary venous return
options.why: Ventilation is not the mechanism either theory describes.

options.t: Direct squeezing of the heart between sternum and spine
options.why: That is the heart pump theory, the competing explanation.

options.t: Pressure changes across the whole chest cavity

questions.stem: In the PEA/asystole algorithm, when is the first epinephrine given?
questions.why: PEA and asystole are not shockable, so the algorithm is CPR for two minutes, then access with 1 mg epi every three to five minutes, an advanced airway with capnography, and the Hs and Ts throughout.

options.t: After two minutes of CPR regardless of access
options.why: The drug still requires a line; access is what gates it.

options.t: As soon as IV or IO access is established
After a defibrillation attempt has been made
options.why: Neither PEA nor asystole is shocked.

options.t: Only after the Hs and Ts have been ruled out
options.why: The Hs and Ts are worked in parallel, not before the first drug.

questions.stem: What findings define symptomatic bradycardia in the program's treatment sheet?
questions.why: A rate under 50 plus evidence the slow rate is costing perfusion: altered mental status, poor skin signs, or a systolic under 90. The goal of treatment is stated simply as increasing the heart rate.

options.t: HR under 40 with systolic under 100
options.why: Both thresholds are lower than the ones on the sheet.

options.t: HR under 60 with any complaint of fatigue
options.why: Under 60 is bradycardia; the treatment sheet uses 50 with objective findings.

options.t: HR under 50 with ALOC, skin signs, or systolic under 90
HR under 50 in any patient, symptoms or not
options.why: The rate alone does not make it symptomatic.

questions.stem: How is atropine dosed for symptomatic bradycardia in this program?
questions.why: 1 mg every three to five minutes, stopping at 3 mg total. If atropine will be delayed you may go straight to pacing, and in that case no 12-lead is required first.

options.t: 1 mg as a single dose only, then pace
options.why: It is repeated to the 3 mg ceiling before pacing becomes the next step.

options.t: 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg
0.5 mg every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg
options.why: The program's unit dose is 1 mg, not 0.5.

options.t: 1 mg every 5 minutes to a maximum of 2 mg
options.why: The ceiling is 3 mg and the interval starts at 3 minutes.

questions.stem: Which bradycardic rhythms does the program say should NOT receive atropine?
questions.why: Atropine works at the AV node. Type II and third-degree blocks sit below it, so the drug cannot help and the delay costs time. Sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest or pause, junctional rhythms, second-degree type I, and idioventricular rhythms are the ones that may get it.

options.t: Second-degree type I and third-degree block
options.why: Type I sits above the block level atropine can influence, so it is on the atropine list.

options.t: Second-degree type II and third-degree block
Sinus bradycardia and sinus arrest
options.why: Both are on the atropine list.

options.t: Junctional and idioventricular rhythms
options.why: Both are listed as rhythms that may receive atropine.

questions.stem: At what rate is transcutaneous pacing set in this program?
questions.why: Pace at 80. Confirm mechanical capture with a pulse that matches the paced rate, not by the spikes on the screen.

options.t: 100 beats per minute
options.why: 100 is faster than the setting used.

options.t: 80 beats per minute
60 beats per minute
options.why: 60 is the low end of normal, below the setting taught.

options.t: Whatever rate restores a palpable pulse
options.why: A specific rate is set and capture is then confirmed against it.

questions.stem: What are the push-dose epinephrine and dopamine ranges on the bradycardia sheet?
questions.why: Push-dose epinephrine is 5 to 20 micrograms as a bolus; dopamine is an infusion at 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min. Both follow atropine and pacing, and the patient goes Code 3 to a cardiac center.

options.t: Epi 100 mcg; dopamine 2 to 5 mcg/kg/min
options.why: Neither figure matches the sheet.

options.t: Epi 5 to 20 mcg; dopamine 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min
Epi 1 to 10 mcg; dopamine 1 to 10 mcg/kg/min
options.why: Both ranges start higher than that.

options.t: Epi 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min; dopamine 5 to 20 mcg
options.why: That swaps the two units — push-dose epi is a bolus in micrograms.

questions.stem: What synchronized cardioversion energies does the program list for a Lifepak versus a Zoll?
questions.why: The escalation depends on the device in your hands. Lifepak goes 100, 200, 300, 360; Zoll goes 100, 150, 200. Know which monitor your service carries.

options.t: Both devices 100, 200, 300, 360
options.why: The Zoll escalation tops out at 200.

options.t: Both devices 50, 100, 200
options.why: Neither device starts at 50 in this program.
That reverses the two device escalations.

questions.stem: A patient in stable SVT has not converted with vagal maneuvers. What comes next, and at what doses?
questions.why: Vagal, then 6 mg adenosine, then 12 mg. If that fails, contact base — the options there are cardioversion or diltiazem. Push it fast at the site closest to the heart with a 20 mL flush.

options.t: Adenosine 12 mg, then 6 mg
options.why: The first dose is the smaller one; it doubles if it fails.

options.t: Adenosine 6 mg, then 6 mg again
options.why: The second dose is doubled rather than repeated.

options.t: Adenosine 6 mg, then 12 mg
Diltiazem first, then adenosine if it fails
options.why: Diltiazem comes later, after base contact.

questions.stem: A patient in stable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. What are the drug options and doses?
questions.why: With a pulse there is time, so amiodarone goes in as 150 mg over ten minutes and lidocaine as an infusion at 1 to 4 mg/min. The same patient without a pulse gets 300 mg of amiodarone as a push.

options.t: Adenosine 6 mg, then 12 mg
options.why: Adenosine is for narrow-complex reentry SVT, not ventricular tachycardia.

options.t: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes, or lidocaine 1 to 4 mg/min
Amiodarone 150 mg push, or lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg push
options.why: With a pulse, amiodarone goes in slowly rather than as a push.

options.t: Amiodarone 300 mg push, or lidocaine 1 to 4 mg/min
options.why: 300 mg push is the arrest dose, for a patient with no pulse.

questions.stem: What is the treatment for stable atrial fibrillation or flutter with a rapid rate?
questions.why: Stable gets diltiazem for rate control. Unstable — hypotensive, poor skin signs, altered — gets synchronized cardioversion regardless of the rhythm's name.

options.t: Adenosine
options.why: Adenosine will not convert atrial fibrillation; the reentry circuit is different.

options.t: Amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes
options.why: That is the stable ventricular tachycardia option.

options.t: Diltiazem
Synchronized cardioversion
options.why: Cardioversion is for the unstable patient in these rhythms.

questions.stem: What three findings define an unstable tachycardia across every rhythm on the sheet?
questions.why: The same triad decides it for SVT, VT, and atrial fibrillation or flutter: hypotension, poor skin signs, altered mental status. Any of the three sends you to synchronized cardioversion.

options.t: A rate over 150 in any rhythm
options.why: Rate alone is a threshold for concern, not the definition of instability.

options.t: A wide QRS with a rate over 100
options.why: A wide complex identifies origin, not stability.

options.t: Hypotension, poor skin signs, and altered mental status
Chest pain of any severity
options.why: Pain matters but is not one of the three findings listed.

questions.stem: The program lists six steps for defibrillation. Which one comes immediately before charging?
questions.why: Standard precautions, prep the skin and apply pads, shave or dry or remove patches as needed, set the energy, charge, then clear and shock — then two minutes of CPR before the next pulse and rhythm check.

options.t: Setting the appropriate energy
Resuming CPR
options.why: CPR resumes after the shock, not before charging.

options.t: Clearing the patient
options.why: Clearing follows charging, immediately before the shock.

options.t: Prepping the skin and applying pads
options.why: Skin prep and pads come earlier, before energy selection.

questions.stem: What compression depth, rate and ratio does the program teach for adult CPR?
questions.why: 2 to 2.4 inches deep, 100 to 120 per minute, 30 compressions to 2 breaths without an advanced airway. With an airway in place, one breath every five to six seconds.

options.t: 2 to 2.4 inches, 100 to 120 per minute, 30:2
1.5 to 2 inches, 100 to 120 per minute, 30:2
options.why: 1.5 inches is the infant depth, not the adult.

options.t: At least 3 inches, 100 to 120 per minute, 30:2
options.why: 3 inches exceeds the depth taught and risks injury.

options.t: 2 to 2.4 inches, 80 to 100 per minute, 15:2
options.why: Both the rate and the ratio are wrong for adult CPR here.

questions.stem: Once CPR has begun, what three events permit you to stop?
questions.why: Start CPR if any doubt exists. Once started, you stop for ROSC, for transfer to another provider, or for a physician assuming responsibility. Withholding it entirely requires obvious signs of death or a DNR.

options.t: ROSC, a family request to stop, or twenty minutes elapsed
options.why: Neither family request nor a fixed clock is on this list.

options.t: ROSC, and no other endpoint is recognized in the field
options.why: Two other endpoints also permit stopping.

options.t: ROSC, arrival at the hospital, or exhaustion of the crew
options.why: Arrival matters only because care is transferred there.

options.t: ROSC, transfer of care, or a physician taking over

questions.stem: Which situations are listed as exceptions to working an arrest on scene, and transporting instead?
questions.why: Extended ACLS, hypothermia, and overdose are the three. The common thread is a reversible cause that hospital resources can address — nobody is dead until warm and dead.

options.t: Hypothermia, pregnancy, and drug overdose
options.why: Pregnancy is not one of the three named.

options.t: Any arrest where the family requests transport
options.why: Family request is not the basis of this list.

options.t: Extended ACLS, hypothermia, and drug overdose
Extended ACLS, pediatric arrest, and trauma
options.why: Neither pediatric arrest nor trauma appears on this exception list.
